```{r}
#| label: setup
library(r2lambda)
```

This article walks through the whole life of a Lambda function: build a
Docker image, test it locally, deploy it, invoke it, run it on a
schedule and delete it. It assumes Docker, curl and AWS credentials are
set up as described in the
[README](https://discindo.github.io/r2lambda/#system-requirements).

## Build a docker image for the lambda function

The examples use two files installed with the package:
`parity.R`, a runtime script whose `parity()` function tells whether a
number is even or odd, and `renv.lock`, an example lockfile.
`system.file()` returns their paths. Replace them with your own script
and lockfile.

```{r}
runtime_function <- "parity"
runtime_path <- system.file("parity.R", package = "r2lambda")
renvlock_path <- system.file("renv.lock", package = "r2lambda")
dependencies <- NULL

# Might take a while, its building a docker image
build_lambda(
  tag = "parity1",
  runtime_function = runtime_function,
  runtime_path = runtime_path,
  renvlock_path = renvlock_path,
  dependencies = dependencies
)
```

`build_lambda()` has a few more options:

- `support_path`: files or folders the runtime script needs. Each is
  copied next to the runtime script under its own name, so
  `support_path = "R"` lets the script call `source("R/helpers.R")`.
- `system_deps`: Amazon Linux 2023 packages to install with `dnf`, for R
  packages that need system libraries, e.g. `system_deps = "udunits2"`
  for `units`. Amazon Linux 2023 has no EPEL, so some libraries, such as
  GDAL, are not available.
- `architecture`: `"x86_64"` (default) or `"arm64"`. `deploy_lambda()`
  creates the function with the image's architecture. Building for an
  architecture other than your machine's needs Docker's QEMU emulation.

## Test the lambda docker image locally

```{r}
payload <- list(number = 2)
test_lambda(tag = "parity1", payload)
```

## Deploy to AWS Lambda

```{r}
# Might take a while, its pushing it to a remote repository
deploy_lambda(tag = "parity1")
```

Lambda stops a function after 3 seconds by default, which an R
container may not meet, especially on its first call. Pass a longer
`Timeout`, in seconds, and other `create_function()` settings through
`...`:

```{r}
deploy_lambda(tag = "parity1", Timeout = 30, MemorySize = 512)
```

The function runs under a new IAM role with basic execution permissions.
To let it call other AWS services, attach policies to that role, or use
a role you already have:

```{r}
deploy_lambda(
  tag = "parity1",
  policy_arns = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess"
)

deploy_lambda(tag = "parity1", role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-role")
```

Inside the function, `paws` picks up the role's temporary credentials,
so no AWS keys go into the image or the function's settings.

## Invoke deployed lambda

```{r}
invoke_lambda(
  function_name = "parity1",
  invocation_type = "RequestResponse",
  payload = list(number = 2),
  include_logs = FALSE
)

#> Lambda response payload:
#> {"parity":"even"}
```

## Run on a schedule

`schedule_lambda()` runs a deployed function at a `rate()` or `cron()`
[schedule
expression](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-create-rule-schedule.html):

```{r}
schedule_lambda("parity1", "rate(5 minutes)")
```

A scheduled run doesn't take a payload. `{lambdr}` passes the `detail`
of the EventBridge event to the handler as arguments, and for a schedule
that is empty, so the handler is called with no arguments. `parity()`
needs `number`, so each scheduled run of `parity1` fails. Give the
arguments of a scheduled handler defaults, e.g.
`parity <- function(number = 2)`.

## Clean up

`delete_lambda()` removes what the steps above created: the function
and its schedules, the execution role, the ECR repository with its
images, the function's log group, and the local Docker image.

```{r}
delete_lambda("parity1")

# Keep the images, for example to deploy them again later
delete_lambda("parity1", keep_ecr_image = TRUE, keep_local_image = TRUE)
```

A role you passed with `deploy_lambda(role_arn = )` is never deleted.
